title: Mr. X & TUSLA
text:
Decision
Mr. X & TUSLA
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-160050-S7Q2N4
Published on 7 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether Tusla was justified in refusing access to records relating to a named deceased individual pursuant to section 37(1) and 37(8) of the Act
7 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 29 April 2025, the applicant sought access to all records held by Tusla (or its predecessor) relating to a named deceased individual. He said the request relates to any complaints, safeguarding concerns, case assessments, or institutional responses connected to the individual.
In a decision dated 29 May 2025, Tusla refused the request. It said the applicant’s request did not fall within the scope of section 37(8) of the FOI Act, which concerns Regulations that provide for the right of access to records of deceased persons by certain categories of individuals. The applicant sought an internal review of Tusla’s decision on 29 May 2025. In its internal review decision dated 19 June 2025, Tusla affirmed its refusal of the request on the ground that the records sought are exempt under section 37(1) of the Act. On 25 June 2025, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of Tusla’s decision.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by both the applicant and Tusla. I have also had regard to the nature and contents of the records at issue. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The scope of this review is concerned solely with whether Tusla was justified in refusing access, under section 37(1) of the FOI Act, to records relating to a named deceased individual.
Preliminary Matters
Before I address the substantive matters arising in this review, I wish to note that this Office has no remit to investigate complaints, to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies. This review has been undertaken under section 22(2) of the Act and is confined to a consideration of whether the decision taken by Tusla on the applicant’s request was justified.
It is also important to note that while I am required by section 22(10) of the FOI Act to give reasons for my decision, section 25(3) provides that the Commissioner must take all reasonable precautions in the performance of his functions to prevent the disclosure of information contained in an exempt record or matter that, if it were included in a record, would cause the record to be an exempt record. Accordingly, the details I can provide of the information redacted in this case are somewhat limited, as are the reasons I can give for my decision.
Lastly, before I proceed to my analysis of the substantive matters relevant to this review, I wish to comment on the nature of the extensive submissions made by the applicant. He has referenced a number of legal authorities and conventions in support of his application. I have carefully considered these authorities and conventions in the context of whether Tusla has justified its decision to rely on the relevant FOI exemption provisions claimed in this case. I wish to observe that general references to legal authorities will often neither assist the applicant in making cogent submissions, nor assist this Office in assessing the submissions made by him. A number of assertions were made by the applicant which, once scrutinised, are not in fact supported by the authorities cited by him. In one such instance, the applicant’s submission refers to what is characterised as a previous decision of this Office which the applicant cited as ‘Mrs Y v Tusla (OIC-170275)’, which the applicant said is supportive of the position that “eligibility under the FOI Regulations is not strictly limited, and that survivors and litigants may obtain access in the public interest”. An investigator from this Office was unable to identify this case by reference to the case number and case name provided and indeed, the applicant was unable to locate a copy of same following a request from this Office. In any event, previous decisions of this Office do not necessarily have precedential value, and this Office must assess each case on its own merits and the factors to be considered as part of any public interest assessment on a case-by-case basis. Therefore, previous decisions of this Office will not necessarily be determinative of subsequent cases. Applicants who prepare submissions for this Office should ensure that their submissions are accurate and that they fairly reflect the authorities cited.
It is worth stating here that this Office has noted an increasing number of cases where submissions are being prepared with the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. Our experience has shown that AI-generated correspondence can be inaccurate and can contain large volumes of material which is irrelevant in the context of the service we provide. Longer, AI-informed documents often lack the clear information we require in order to assess the issue involved. Instead, they often provide a substantial amount of additional information which does not help us deal with a case and, generally, these cases take longer to deal with.
Analysis and Findings
Section 37(1) & 37(7)
Section 37(1) of the FOI Act provides that, subject to the other provisions of the section, an FOI body shall refuse a request if access to the record concerned would involve the disclosure of personal information, including personal information relating to a deceased individual. This does not apply where the information involved relates to the requester (section 37(2)(a) refers). However, section 37(7) provides that, notwithstanding section 37(2)(a), an FOI body shall refuse to grant a request if access to the record concerned would, in addition to involving the disclosure of personal information relating to the requester, also involve the disclosure of personal information relating to an individual or individuals other than the requester (commonly known as joint personal information). Essentially, this means that while section 37(1) does not provide a basis for refusing access to personal information that relates solely to the requester, the request shall be refused pursuant to section 37(7) if that personal information is inextricably linked to personal information relating to parties other than the applicant.
Section 2 of the Act defines ‘personal information’ as information about an identifiable individual that, either (a) would, in the ordinary course of events, be known only to the individual or members of the family, or friends, of the individual, or (b) is held by the FOI body on the understanding that it would be treated by that body as confidential. Section 2 goes on to specify 14 categories of information which, without prejudice to the generality of the definition provided for under section 2, comprises personal information, these include (i) information relating to the educational, medical, psychiatric or psychological history of the individual, (vi) information relating to any criminal history of, or the commission or alleged commission of any offence by, the individual, and (xiv) the views or opinions of another person about the individual.
Having reviewed the records concerned, I am satisfied that they are records to which section 37(1) applies. I am not, unfortunately, in a position to provide a more detailed description of the information contained in the records in light of the requirement in section 25(3) of the Act that the Commissioner must take all reasonable precautions in the performance of his functions to prevent the disclosure of exempt information. Suffice to say, the records are of a highly sensitive and personal nature. Furthermore, having reviewed the records concerned, I am satisfied that the records to which section 37(7) applies are of a kind whereby the personal information of the applicant is inextricably linked to other individuals, and that section 37(7) applies to those records.
However, that is not the end of the matter, however, as section 37(1) is subject to the other provisions of section 37.
Section 37(2)
Section 37(2) of the FOI Act provides that section 37(1) does not apply if:
(a) subject to subsection (3), the information concerned relates to the requester concerned,
(b) any individual to whom the information relates consents, in writing or such other form as may be determined, to its disclosure to the requester,
(c) information of the same kind as that contained in the record in respect of individuals generally, or a class of individuals that is, having regard to all the circumstances, of significant size, is available to the general public,
(d) the information was given to the FOI body concerned by the individual to whom it relates and the individual was informed on behalf of the body, before its being so given, that the information belongs to a class of information that would or might be made available to the general public, or
(e) disclosure of the information is necessary in order to avoid a serious and imminent danger to the life or health of an individual,
In its submissions to this Office Tusla submitted that none of the provisions of section 37(2) apply to the records concerned. Having reviewed the records myself, some information contained in certain of the records contain information relating to the applicant. Save for those specific records, which I have considered in the context of section 37(7) above, I am satisfied that none of the provision of section 37(2) apply to the balance of the withheld records.
Section 37(5)
Section 37(5) provides that a request which would otherwise be refused under section 37(1) may be granted where on balance (a) the public interest that the request be granted outweighs the public interest that the right to privacy of the individual to whom the information relates should be upheld, or (b) the grant of the request would benefit the person to whom the information relates. I am satisfied that section 37(5)(b) does not apply in this case.
Before I consider the applicability of section 37(5)(a), there are a number of important points to note. First, section 13(4) provides that in deciding whether to grant or refuse an FOI request, any reason that the applicant gives for the request and any belief or opinion of the FOI body as to the reasons for the request shall be disregarded. In relation to the question of the public interest, this means that I cannot have regard to the applicant's motives for seeking access to the records at issue, except in so far as those motives reflect, or overlap with, what might be regarded as true public interest factors in favour of release of the records, i.e. insofar as the concerns raised in relation to the request may also be matters of general concern to the wider public.
Secondly, it is important to note when records are released under the FOI Act they are considered, in effect, to be released to the world at large, as the Act places no constraints on the uses to which a released record under the Act can be put. With certain limited exceptions provided for under the Act, FOI is not about granting access to information to particular individuals only and as noted above, an applicant's reasons for making a request are generally not of relevance. Thus, records are not released under FOI for any limited or restricted purpose.
All of this means that in considering whether a right of access exists to records under section 37(5)(a) of the Act, any decision to grant access would be on the basis that there is an overriding public interest in the release of the records effectively to the world at large that outweighs the privacy rights of the third party individuals concerned.
In considering where the balance of the public interest lies in this case, I have had regard to section 11(3) of the Act which provides that in performing any functions under the Act, an FOI body must have regard to, among other things, the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. However, in doing so, I have also had regard to the judgment of the Supreme Court in The Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources and the Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57. In that case, the Supreme Court found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and “there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”. Although the Court’s comments were made in a case involving commercial sensitivity and confidentiality, I consider them to be relevant to the consideration of public interest tests generally.
In its internal review decision, Tusla said that it considered the following factors in favour of release of the records in question:
• The public interest in openness, transparency and accountability in the manner in which Tusla performs its functions.
• The public interest in members of the public knowing that the information held by public bodies about them, or those they represent is accurate.
• The public interest in members of the public exercising their rights under the FOI Act.
Tusla said it considered the following factors against release of the records sought:
• The public interest in protecting the right to privacy.
I accept that in this case, the applicant has made a complaint to Tusla concerning the named individual and that there is a public interest in the applicant being aware of how Tusla have handled his case and what (if any) investigations it has carried out on foot of same. Having had regard to the withheld records, it appears that the applicant has been made aware of what occurred in respect of his complaint and why Tusla ceased to have a role in any investigation.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant made reference to a number of legal authorities including the Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (“the Lanzarote Convention”), the Children First Act 2015. The applicant said these authorities support the proposition that the public interest favours the release of the records sought as he said that the records concern safeguarding transparency, systemic accountability, and the right to justice in abuse cases. The applicant has not cited any specific provisions of either authority, simply referring to them in a general way.
The applicant also made reference to jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, namely its decisions in Gaskin v United Kingdom App no. 10454/83 (ECtHR, 7 July 1989) and O’Keeffe v Ireland App no. 35810/09 (ECtHR, 28 January 2014). The applicant said that these decisions were supportive of the proposition that there exists a right of access to ‘institutional records’ where child protection responsibilities were exercised and where such access is essential to legal redress. Following a review of these decisions, I am satisfied that these decisions do not create an unfettered right of access to records.
In any event, I have considered the content of the authorities cited by the applicant insofar as they could possibly relate to his entitlement to request access to records under FOI legislation. To that end, I find that the applicant’s submissions in that regard relate to the public interest in survivors of abuse being able to understand the steps taken by Tusla in handling and investigating their complaints.
Additionally, the applicant also said that there were a number of additional factors which favoured release of the records:
• He said that the High Court has already found special circumstances under section 27(4) of the Succession Act 1965, which led to the appointment of an independent administrator ad litem.
• He said that through an affidavit sworn by him, the Court is aware of multiple victims of the deceased individual and a pattern of abuse spanning a 20-year age gap.
• He said that Tusla records are directly relevant to establishing that pattern and to ensuring that the administration of the estate is conducted with full transparency in the context of live High Court proceedings.
These additional factors proffered by the applicant relate to the existence of High Court proceedings brought by him against the estate of the deceased. Those proceedings have not concluded, and I note that the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the deceased’s estate is “limited for the purposes of substantiating proceedings to be brought by the [applicant]”. The weight to be afforded to such factors when considering the public interest is, in my view, somewhat limited and personal in nature, since it is the applicant who has brought proceedings against the estate of the individual the subject of his request.
What remains to be considered, therefore, is information concerning third parties. The FOI Act recognises the public interest in the protection of the right to privacy both in the language of section 37 and the Long Title to the Act (which makes clear that the release of records under FOI must be consistent with the right to privacy). It is also worth noting that the right to privacy has a constitutional dimension, as one of the unenumerated personal rights under the Constitution. Moreover, unlike other public interest tests provided for in the FOI Act, there is a discretionary element to section 37(5)(a), which is a further indication of the very strong public interest in the right to privacy. Privacy rights will therefore be set aside only where the public interest served by granting the request (and breaching those rights) is sufficiently strong to outweigh the public interest in protecting privacy.
In light of the foregoing, I am satisfied that given the nature of the records at issue, which concern allegations of a most serious nature against the deceased individual, that there is even greater weight to be afforded to the right to privacy of third party individuals than would be the case in the ordinary course. The weight to be afforded to the right to privacy is already a significant one, and particularly so where release under FOI is, potentially at least, release to the world at large. I am not satisfied that there is a specific, cogent and fact-based reason which would outweigh the strong protection to be afforded to the right to privacy of any third parties in this case. I find, therefore, that section 37(5)(a) does not apply.
Section 37(8)
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant submitted that he is entitled to the records pursuant to section 37(8) of the Act. Section 37(8) of the Act provides that, notwithstanding subsection (1), the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform may provide by regulations for the grant of an FOI request where the individual to whom the record concerned relates is dead and the requester concerned is a member of a class specified in the regulations.
The Freedom of Information Act 2014 (Section 37(8)) Regulations 2016 (S.I. No. 218 of 2016), as amended, are the relevant Regulations in this case (“the Regulations”). Amongst other things, the Regulations provide that, notwithstanding section 37(1) (and subject to the other provisions of the FOI Act), a request for records which involves the disclosure of personal information of a deceased individual shall be granted where the requester is a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the individual or his or her estate acting in the course of the performance of the function.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant said that he is such a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the estate of the individual. To that end, the applicant submitted that he is the plaintiff in proceedings brought against the estate of the individual the subject of this request. In particular, the applicant cited the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the deceased’s estate by the High Court. The applicant provided a copy of the relevant Court order which identifies the administrator ad litem (who is a solicitor) and notes that the administrator ad litem’s appointment is “ limited for the purposes of substantiating proceedings to be brought by the [applicant
]”.
Tusla do not accept that the applicant belongs to a class of individual to whom section 37(8) and the Regulations apply. I should observe at this juncture that the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the estate occurred subsequent to the applicant’s application to this Office for a review. However, Tusla submitted that this development does not materially change matters.
The Regulations provide that a request for a record which involves the disclosure of personal information shall, subject to the other provisions of the Act, be granted where the individual to whom the record relates is dead and the requester is a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the individual or his or her estate acting in the course of the performance of the function. Having considered the applicant’s submissions, I am satisfied that the applicant is not such an individual.
Prior to the appointment of the administrator ad litem, the applicant also said that his status as a complainant against the deceased individual and as a plaintiff in proceedings brought against the deceased’s estate conferred him with a function by law in respect of the deceased’s estate. I am satisfied that this could not possibly be the case. Quite apart from the fact that no “function” is conferred by law on the applicant, since it was he himself who made the complaint and initiated proceedings against the estate, if what the applicant contended was correct, any individual wishing to obtain sensitive records concerning a deceased individual need only initiate legal proceedings or make a complaint against that individual or his estate. I am satisfied that on no reading of the Regulations could this be the case.
Accordingly, in light of the foregoing, I have found that section 37(1) serves to exempt from release the records which the applicant seeks. The applicant has not demonstrated that he belongs to any category of individual set out in the Regulations and accordingly section 37(8) does not serve to disapply section 37(1).
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm Tusla’s decision. I find that Tusla was justified in refusing access to the records sought pursuant to section 37(1).
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator
